Clinical Reference

Community-Acquired Pneumonia (v2)

On this page
Acute infection of the lung parenchyma acquired outside the hospital — a compatible clinical syndrome (cough, fever, dyspnea, pleuritic pain) plus a new infiltrate on chest imaging. Pick the site of care with a severity score, then cover the likely bugs.
Guideline: ATS/IDSA 2019 (Metlay) Top pathogen: S. pneumoniae Disposition: PSI / CURB-65 + judgment Severe = 1 major or ≥3 minor → ICU Min. duration: 5 days
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Pathogens reach the alveoli mainly by micro-aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions (the dominant route for S. pneumoniae) or by inhalation of aerosols (Legionella, Mycoplasma, viruses). Disease begins when inoculum and virulence overwhelm host defenses — mucociliary clearance, cough, secretory IgA, surfactant, and the alveolar macrophage.

Once organisms land in the alveolus, their PAMPs (pneumococcal peptidoglycan/lipoteichoic acid, gram-negative LPS) trip alveolar-macrophage pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs). The macrophage releases IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-8. IL-8 and TNF pull neutrophils out of the pulmonary capillaries into the air space; the same mediators make the alveolar–capillary membrane leaky. Alveoli fill with protein-rich exudate, fibrin, neutrophils, and red cells → consolidation. Those alveoli are still perfused but no longer ventilated, so blood passes without picking up oxygen — an intrapulmonary shunt / V̇/Q̇ mismatch that produces hypoxemia relatively resistant to supplemental O₂. Meanwhile IL-1/IL-6/TNF act systemically → fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, rising CRP/procalcitonin, and — if unchecked — the sepsis cascade.

Fluid-filled alveoli transmit sound better than air, which is why consolidation gives bronchial breath sounds, increased tactile fremitus, egophony (E→A), whispered pectoriloquy, dullness to percussion, and — from airway/alveolar fluid — crackles. On imaging: lobar or patchy air-space opacity, air bronchograms, ± parapneumonic effusion.

An alveolus is a tiny room that must stay full of air to load oxygen onto passing blood. Bacteria are intruders; the alveolar macrophage is the security guard who trips the fire alarm (cytokines). Firefighters (neutrophils) flood the room with water (exudate) to drown the intruders — but a water-filled room can't hold air, so oxygen can't reach the blood flowing past (shunt → hypoxemia). Antibiotics are targeted strikes on the intruders: β-lactams blow up their walls; macrolides, doxycycline, and quinolones jam their factories and blueprints so they can't rebuild.

CAP inflammatory cascade — where each therapy class intervenes. Diagram adapts to light/dark theme.
Normal alveoli — thin air-filled sacs where gas exchange occurs. In CAP these fill with protein-rich exudate, fibrin, and neutrophils (consolidation).
Cruithne9 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Alveolus.jpg
Every antibiotic in this guide maps to one step above. β-lactams (amoxicillin, ampicillin/sulbactam, ceftriaxone, cefepime, pip-tazo, ceftaroline) bind penicillin-binding proteins → block peptidoglycan cross-linking → the wall fails and the organism lyses — but atypicals lack that wall, so β-lactams miss them. Macrolides (azithromycin) bind the 50S ribosome to stop protein synthesis and down-regulate cytokines. Doxycycline binds the 30S ribosome. Respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV. That is why CAP regimens pair a wall-active β-lactam with an atypical agent — or use a fluoroquinolone that covers both.
🗂️

Classification & the usual bugs

CAP vs HAP vs VAP

CategoryDefinitionNote
CAPPneumonia acquired outside hospital; not hospitalized/in long-term care ≥48 h before onsetThis guide (ATS/IDSA 2019)
HAPPneumonia ≥48 h after admission, not incubating on arrival2016 ATS/IDSA HAP/VAP guideline
VAPPneumonia >48 h after endotracheal intubationSeparate empirics
"HCAP" is dead. The 2005 healthcare-associated-pneumonia category was abandoned in 2019 — it poorly predicted resistant organisms and drove massive over-use of vancomycin + antipseudomonal β-lactams. Cover MRSA/Pseudomonas only for validated risk factors (below), not because a patient is old, comorbid, or from a nursing home.

Typical vs atypical vs viral

GroupOrganismsWhy it matters for drug choice
Typical bacteriaS. pneumoniae (most common), H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. aureus (incl. MRSA), group A strep, aerobic GNRHave a cell wall → covered by β-lactams
Atypical bacteriaMycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophilaNo/atypical wall or intracellular → β-lactams miss them → need macrolide, doxycycline, or fluoroquinolone
VirusesInfluenza A/B, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, rhinovirus, hMPV, parainfluenza, adenovirusCommon cause & co-pathogen — test & treat influenza/COVID when circulating
Risk-definedPseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA (risk factors), anaerobes (abscess/empyema)Add coverage only when validated risk present
When to add MRSA / Pseudomonas coverage: the two strongest predictors are (1) prior respiratory isolation of that organism, or (2) hospitalization AND parenteral antibiotics within the last 90 days — weighted by local antibiogram and severity. Get cultures and de-escalate at 48 h if negative.

Pathogen-specific clues (and the agent that covers them)

OrganismClue / settingPreferred coverage
S. pneumoniaeRusty sputum, single rigor, lobar consolidation, aspleniaβ-lactam (amoxicillin/ceftriaxone)
MycoplasmaYoung adult, dry cough, headache/myalgia, bullous myringitis, cold agglutinins, "walking pneumonia"Macrolide, doxycycline, or FQ
LegionellaGI symptoms/diarrhea, hyponatremia, ↑LFTs, relative bradycardia, water-aerosol/travel exposureFQ or azithromycin; send urinary antigen
H. influenzae / M. catarrhalisCOPD / smokersAmox/clav, cephalosporin, FQ
KlebsiellaAlcoholism, "currant-jelly" sputum, upper-lobe bulging fissure, cavitationβ-lactam per susceptibilities
MRSAPost-influenza, necrotizing/cavitary, hemoptysis, empyema; prior isolationVancomycin or linezolid
AnaerobesAspiration + abscess/empyema, poor dentition, putrid sputumAmp/sulbactam or add anaerobic agent (only if abscess/empyema)
Influenza / SARS-CoV-2Seasonal, myalgia/anosmia, bilateral ground-glassOseltamivir / antivirals + treat bacterial co-infection

The four classic stages of lobar pneumonia

StageTimingWhat's happening
1 · CongestionDay 1–2Vascular engorgement, serous exudate, bacteria proliferate; heavy, red, boggy lobe
2 · Red hepatizationDay 2–4Alveoli packed with RBCs, neutrophils, fibrin → lung looks liver-like (red, firm, airless)
3 · Gray hepatizationDay 4–6RBCs break down, fibrinosuppurative exudate persists → gray-brown, still firm
4 · ResolutionDay 8+Macrophages clear exudate, enzymes digest debris, architecture restored (or organizes if it fails)
This is why the CXR lags the clinical picture: radiographic clearing can take up to 6 weeks, so a persistent opacity in a patient who feels well is expected — don't re-treat a picture, treat the patient.
📊

Presentation — how often, and why

Approximate frequency in adult CAP. ■ >70% · ■ 40–70% · ■ 15–40% · ■ <15%. Elderly patients often present atypically (confusion, falls, decompensated comorbidity, minimal fever).

Symptom / sign~FreqWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Cough (± productive)~80%Airway/alveolar exudate irritates cough receptors; sputum = purulent inflammatory debris
Fatigue / malaise~80%Systemic IL-1/IL-6/TNF cytokine effect
Fever / chills~75%IL-1/IL-6/TNF reset the hypothalamic set-point; rigors track bacteremia
Crackles / rales on exam~75%Air bubbling through fluid-filled distal airways/alveoli
Dyspnea~65%Shunt physiology → hypoxemia → ↑respiratory drive; loss of compliant lung
Sputum production~60%Neutrophil-rich exudate mobilized from consolidated alveoli
Tachypnea (RR ≥20–30)~50%Chemoreceptor response to hypoxemia and metabolic demand; a key severity sign
Pleuritic chest pain~45%Inflammation reaching the visceral/parietal pleura; more with peripheral consolidation/effusion
Tachycardia (HR ≥100)~45%Fever, hypoxemia, cytokine-driven sympathetic tone, hypovolemia
Bronchial breath sounds / egophony / dullness~30%Consolidated lung transmits sound better than air; ↑fremitus, E→A change, percussion dullness
GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea)~25%Systemic inflammation; diarrhea classically with Legionella
Confusion / delirium~20%Hypoxemia, sepsis, and cytokines — much more common (and sometimes the only clue) in elderly; a CURB-65 point
Hemoptysis~12%Alveolar capillary disruption; also seen with necrotizing/MRSA pneumonia
Hypotension (SBP <90)~10%Sepsis-driven vasodilation ± hypovolemia — a severity/ICU trigger

🩺 Clinic — outpatient diagnosis, treatment & prevention
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Outpatient presentation & risk

Acute cough (often productive), fever/chills, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachypnea, and focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds. Ask about duration, sick contacts, travel, aspiration risk, vaccination status, prior MRSA/Pseudomonas, recent hospitalization/antibiotics, and comorbidities.

  • Higher-risk hosts: age ≥65, COPD/asthma, CHF, diabetes, CKD, chronic liver disease, alcohol-use disorder, malignancy, asplenia, immunosuppression, smoking.
  • Atypical clue set: younger patient, dry cough, headache, myalgia, extrapulmonary features (diarrhea → Legionella; bullous myringitis / cold agglutinins → Mycoplasma).
In the elderly, pneumonia can present as confusion, a fall, or "just not right" with little or no fever — a low threshold to image and check a pulse oximetry saves lives.

Score

Severity & site-of-care

🧮

CURB-65 (interactive)

1 point each. Lim et al., Thorax 2003. Use alongside clinical judgment — ATS/IDSA 2019 actually prefers the PSI/PORT for the admit decision (link below).

C — New confusion / disorientation
U — Urea >7 mmol/L (BUN >19 mg/dL)
R — Respiratory rate ≥30/min
B — SBP <90 or DBP ≤60 mmHg
65 — Age ≥65 years
0
Select the criteria that apply.
0–1 → outpatient usually appropriate. 2 → short admission or close observation. ≥3 → admit and assess for ICU (4–5 = high mortality). CRB-65 (drop urea) works when no labs are available in clinic.

The 20-variable PSI/PORT nomogram is better for confirming a patient is low-risk enough for home, but its point math is too complex to reproduce reliably here — compute PSI/PORT on MDCalc →. Classes I–II (≤70 pts) ≈ outpatient; III (71–90) outpatient/observation; IV (91–130) inpatient; V (>130) inpatient ± ICU.

Outpatient antibiotic therapy

💊

Empiric ladder — healthy → comorbid → escalate

Outpatient CAP is dominated by S. pneumoniae and atypicals. The healthy-host regimens each cover the likely spectrum; comorbid hosts get a β-lactam (for resistant pneumococcus/H. influenzae) plus an atypical agent, or a single respiratory fluoroquinolone that does both.

Choose ONE monotherapy

Azithromycin (macrolide)500 mg PO day 1, then 250 mg daily ×4Only if local pneumococcal macrolide resistance <25% (often NOT true in US, >30%)50S ribosome + anti-inflammatoryClarithromycin 500 mg BID / ER 1 g daily

DrugStart / doseNotesWhy it worksCautions
Levofloxacin750 mg PO dailyRenal-dose if CrCl <50DNA gyrase/topo IV inhibitionQT, tendinopathy, aortic, dysglycemia, CNS, C. diff

Reserve fluoroquinolones when a β-lactam+macrolide will do — they carry black-box tendon/aortic/CNS warnings and can mask/delay a TB diagnosis. But for a true penicillin allergy they are the clean single-agent answer.
3
Not improving at 48–72 h / can't take PO / hypoxic
Escalate site of care
▾

Re-image, reconsider the diagnosis (CHF, PE, malignancy, TB, empyema, resistant/atypical organism, viral), and admit if SpO₂ <92%, RR ≥30, SBP <90, new confusion, unable to tolerate oral meds, or CURB-65 ≥2 / PSI III–V. Switch to inpatient regimens (see Wards).

DurationMinimum 5 days, and continue only until the patient is afebrile 48–72 h and clinically stable (normalizing HR, RR, SBP, SpO₂, temp, mentation, able to eat). Longer courses are for documented complications only. No routine follow-up CXR in patients improving clinically.
Monitor

Follow-up

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • 48–72 h: phone or in-person check — expect defervescence and less cough/dyspnea. Failure to improve → re-evaluate/escalate.
  • Follow-up CXR: not routine to prove resolution; consider at 6–12 weeks in smokers ≥50 or those at cancer risk to exclude an obstructing lesion.
  • Smoking cessation and ensure vaccines are up to date at the recovery visit.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B recommendations relevant to CAP risk

GradeRecommendationPopulation
ATobacco cessation — ask, advise, and offer behavioral counseling + FDA-approved pharmacotherapyAll adults who use tobacco (biggest modifiable CAP risk)
BScreen for unhealthy alcohol use & brief counselingAdults ≥18 (alcohol-use disorder raises CAP risk/severity)
BLung cancer screening — annual low-dose CTAges 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, currently smoke or quit <15 y

Vaccination (CDC/ACIP — the core CAP prevention)

  • Pneumococcal: per the 2024 ACIP update, all adults ≥50 (and 19–49 with risk conditions) — PCV20 or PCV21 alone, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23.
  • Influenza: annual, everyone ≥6 months.
  • COVID-19: per current recommendations.
  • RSV: adults ≥75, and 60–74 with risk factors.
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

SpO₂ <92% on room air · RR ≥30 · SBP <90 · new confusion · inability to tolerate oral intake · hemoptysis · multilobar infiltrate · rapid deterioration · failure to improve after 48–72 h of appropriate therapy · CURB-65 ≥2 or PSI class IV–V.
🛏️ Wards — non-severe inpatient CAP
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & profile

  • CURB-65 ≥2 or PSI class III–V (use score + judgment; ATS/IDSA prefers PSI for this decision).
  • Hypoxia (SpO₂ <92% / new O₂ requirement), hemodynamic instability, inability to take/absorb oral meds, decompensated comorbidity, failed outpatient therapy, or unsafe social circumstances.
Screen for severe CAP at the door (see ICU tab): 1 major or ≥3 minor criteria means ICU, not the floor.

3
Adjuncts & special situations
Steroids, influenza, effusion
▾
  • Corticosteroids: not routine for non-severe CAP (ATS/IDSA 2019). Use only for a separate indication (COPD exacerbation, refractory septic shock). Severe ICU-level CAP is different — see CAPE COD on the ICU tab.
  • Influenza-positive: add oseltamivir 75 mg PO BID for hospitalized patients regardless of symptom duration; continue antibacterials (bacterial co-infection common).
  • Complicated parapneumonic effusion / empyema: pleural drainage; consider intrapleural tPA/DNase; extend antibiotic duration.
DurationMinimum 5 days; stop once clinically stable + afebrile 48–72 h. Extend only for empyema/abscess, metastatic infection, or Pseudomonas/MRSA. Procalcitonin can support earlier discontinuation in improving patients (adjunct, not a mandate).
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend & IV→PO switch

Trend daily: temperature, HR, RR, SpO₂/O₂ requirement, SBP/MAP, mental status, WBC, renal function, ability to eat, and lactate if it was elevated.

Switch IV → PO when: hemodynamically stable, clinically improving, able to take oral meds, and a functioning GI tract (usually 48–72 h). Use the same or an equivalent oral agent, then plan discharge — don't reflexively hold discharge to watch the first oral dose.

IV agentOral step-downNote
Ceftriaxone + azithromycinAmox/clav 875/125 BID (or cefpodoxime/cefuroxime) + azithromycin POOr step to a respiratory FQ to consolidate to one pill
Ampicillin/sulbactamAmoxicillin/clavulanate POSame spectrum orally
Levofloxacin IVLevofloxacin 750 mg PO~100% oral bioavailability — same dose
Moxifloxacin IVMoxifloxacin 400 mg POHigh bioavailability — same dose
Azithromycin IVAzithromycin 500 mg POSame dose
Vancomycin IV (MRSA)Linezolid 600 mg POLinezolid is orally bioavailable; vancomycin PO is not systemically absorbed
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers (numeric)

Any major severe-CAP criterion: vasopressor-dependent shock or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation. Or ≥3 minor criteria: RR ≥30 · PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤250 · multilobar infiltrates · confusion · BUN ≥20 · WBC <4,000 · platelets <100,000 · temp <36 °C · hypotension needing aggressive fluids. Also: rising lactate, worsening hypoxemia despite escalating O₂, or new multilobar spread.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: afebrile, stable vitals, SpO₂ ≥90% on room air (or stable home O₂), tolerating oral antibiotics/intake, stable mentation, and a safe follow-up plan. Meeting these = ready even if a small infiltrate persists.

Home

Independent, stable on oral therapy, reliable follow-up.

Home health

Home + skilled nursing/therapy or short-course IV/O₂ support.

SNF

Needs 24 h skilled nursing, deconditioned, <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care (e.g., vent weaning) >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Recurrent aspiration/end-stage disease; comfort-focused goals.

Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, cultures, targets

  • Access: arterial line for beat-to-beat BP/ABGs if shock or ventilated; central line for vasopressors.
  • Full micro (severe CAP): blood cultures, sputum culture/Gram stain, urinary pneumococcal + Legionella antigens, respiratory viral testing (influenza/SARS-CoV-2). Consider MRSA nares PCR to help de-escalate vancomycin.
  • Trend: lactate/clearance, ScvO₂ if available, urine output, MAP ≥65, PaO₂/FiO₂, WBC/platelets, renal & hepatic function, glucose (esp. if on steroids).
Legionella pneumophila — a severe-CAP atypical (diarrhea, hyponatremia, ↑LFTs, relative bradycardia). Send urinary antigen in severe/ICU CAP.
CDC (PHIL #1187) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons: Legionella pneumophila 01.jpg

Adjunct

Corticosteroids — CAPE COD

💉

Hydrocortisone in ICU-level severe CAP

CAPE COD (Dequin, NEJM 2023) — 31 French ICUs, ~800 adults with severe CAP (PSI >130, or mechanical ventilation, or high-flow O₂ with FiO₂ ≥0.5 & PaO₂/FiO₂ <300); influenza and septic shock as a required feature excluded.

RegimenResult
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV continuous infusion, started within ~24 h. Day-4 assessment: if improved → 4-day course then taper (total 8 d); if not → continue to day 7 then taper (total 14 d).28-day mortality 6.2% vs 11.9% (−5.6 pp, P=0.006, NNT ≈18); fewer intubations (18.0% vs 29.5%) and less vasopressor initiation (15.3% vs 25.0%). More hyperglycemia/insulin need; no significant excess infection or GI bleed.
CAPE COD has shifted practice toward hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for ICU-level severe CAP without contraindication (avoid in active influenza/uncontrolled infection). Contrast ESCAPe (2022): low-dose methylprednisolone ×20 days was negative for 60-day mortality — agent, dose, timing, and population matter. ATS/IDSA 2019 predates CAPE COD and still lists steroids as non-routine, reserved for refractory septic shock.
Support

Pressors & septic shock

🩹

Which drip, why, and the dose (Surviving Sepsis 2021)

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 >> β1~0.02–0.5+ mcg/kg/min, titrate to MAP ≥65↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line in septic shock
VasopressinV1 vasoconstrictionFixed 0.03 units/min (add-on, not titrated)↑SVR, catecholamine-sparingAdd to norepi to raise MAP / lower catecholamine dose
Epinephrineβ1 = α1 > β2~0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↑SVR (↑lactate)Second/third-line add-on
HydrocortisoneGlucocorticoid — restores vascular tone200 mg/day IVPressor-sparingShock refractory to fluids + pressors
Septic-shock hypotension is pathological vasodilation, so the goal is to restore systemic vascular resistance — hence an α1 agonist (norepinephrine) first. Vasopressin acts through a non-adrenergic (V1) pathway to add tone without more catecholamine. Give ~30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypoperfusion, then reassess with dynamic measures rather than chasing a fixed number.
Airway

Respiratory support & vent

🌬️

Oxygen → HFNC/NIV → intubate; ARDSNet settings

Escalate O₂ to keep SpO₂ 92–96% (88–92% in chronic hypercapnia). High-flow nasal cannula is often first for hypoxemic respiratory failure; NIV can help selected patients but watch for failure. Intubate for a major criterion (respiratory failure), worsening hypoxemia/work of breathing, or altered mentation. Pneumonia is a leading cause of ARDS — ventilate lung-protectively.

Rescue

Advanced / refractory options

⚙️

When lung-protective ventilation isn't enough

  • Prone positioning ≥16 h/day for moderate–severe ARDS (P/F <150).
  • Neuromuscular blockade for severe dyssynchrony/refractory hypoxemia.
  • Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide/epoprostenol) as a bridge.
  • VV-ECMO referral for refractory hypoxemia (e.g., P/F <80 or uncompensated hypercapnia despite optimization).
  • Source control: drain empyema; débride/drain lung abscess if not resolving.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Transfer out when: off vasopressors, improving oxygenation and weaning O₂/extubated, afebrile with stable mentation, antibiotics de-escalated to targeted therapy per cultures, and tolerating enteral intake with an IV→PO plan. Not yet if: still needing pressors or high-flow/vent support, lactate not clearing, or new organ dysfunction. Consider LTAC for prolonged vent weaning, and revisit goals of care in patients with poor prognosis or recurrent aspiration.

Differential — CAP mimics

🧭

"It's not improving" — reconsider the diagnosis

Roughly 10–15% of "CAP not responding at 72 h" is a wrong or incomplete diagnosis. Before broadening antibiotics, ask what else fills or shadows the lung.

MimicDistinguishing clueTest
Acute heart failure / pulmonary edemaOrthopnea, PND, JVD, S3, bilateral symmetric infiltrates, cardiomegaly, no feverBNP/NT-proBNP, echo, diuretic response
Pulmonary embolismPleuritic pain + hypoxia with clear/near-clear CXR, risk factors, tachycardia out of proportionD-dimer / CT-PA
Aspiration chemical pneumonitisRapid onset after a witnessed aspiration event; often resolves without antibioticsHistory, dependent-segment infiltrate
Lung cancer / post-obstructive pneumoniaSmoker, weight loss, hemoptysis, recurrent same-lobe pneumonia, non-resolving opacityCT ± bronchoscopy; follow-up CXR 6–12 wk
TuberculosisSubacute cough >2–3 wk, night sweats, weight loss, upper-lobe/cavitary, exposureAFB smear/culture, NAAT, isolate
Organizing pneumonia (COP)Migratory infiltrates not responding to antibiotics; steroid-responsiveCT pattern, biopsy
Empyema / abscessPersistent fever/leukocytosis despite antibiotics, loculated effusion, cavitationCT, thoracentesis (pH <7.2 → drain)
COVID-19 / viral pneumonitisBilateral peripheral ground-glass, anosmia, exposurePCR/antigen
Two common traps: giving antibiotics for pure CHF (they don't help and delay diuresis), and stopping too early on a "resolving" empyema — a persistently spiking fever on adequate antibiotics means look for undrained pus.

Comorbidities & drug cautions

🔗

How comorbidities change the course & the plan

ComorbidityHow it changes CAPManagement adjustment
COPD↑Pseudomonas risk (frequent exacerbations, steroids, bronchiectasis); CO₂ retention risk with O₂Consider antipseudomonal cover if risk factors; systemic steroids for concurrent COPD exacerbation; target SpO₂ 88–92%
CHFMimics and coexists with CAP (dyspnea, crackles, infiltrate/effusion)Use BNP/echo/context to distinguish; careful fluid balance — resuscitate sepsis but avoid pulmonary edema; diurese once stable/euvolemic
CKD / ESRDHigher severity; drug accumulationRenal-dose levofloxacin, cefepime, pip-tazo, meropenem, vancomycin (level-guided). No adjust: azithromycin, moxifloxacin, ceftriaxone, doxycycline. Watch cefepime neurotoxicity
Diabetes↑severity; steroids worsen hyperglycemiaMonitor glucose/insulin closely (esp. on CAPE COD steroids)
ImmunosuppressionBroadens differential (PJP, fungi, CMV, Nocardia, resistant GNR) — outside standard CAP empiricsInvolve ID; expand workup and coverage
Aspiration risk (stroke, dementia, dysphagia)Recurrent lower-lobe/dependent pneumoniaStandard CAP regimens; add anaerobic cover only for abscess/empyema; SLP swallow eval
CirrhosisImmune dysfunction → ↑severity & bacteremiaCaution with hepatotoxic/QT drugs; adjust as needed
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: Fluoroquinolones — QT prolongation, tendinopathy/rupture, aortic aneurysm/dissection, dys­glycemia, CNS (seizure/delirium/neuropathy), C. difficile; avoid stacking QT drugs; can delay a TB diagnosis. Macrolides — QT prolongation; clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor (statins, warfarin, etc.). Aminoglycosides — nephro/ototoxicity; avoid unless necessary, level-guided. Cefepime — encephalopathy/myoclonus/non-convulsive status in under-dosed CKD. Vancomycin — nephrotoxicity, AUC/level-guided. Doxycycline — photosensitivity, pill esophagitis (take upright with water), avoid in pregnancy.

Renal dose adjustment — quick reference

DrugRenal adjustment
Amoxicillin / amox-clavReduce/extend interval if CrCl <30
LevofloxacinCrCl 20–49 → 750 mg q48h; CrCl <20 → 750 mg ×1 then 500 mg q48h
MoxifloxacinNo adjustment (hepatic clearance)
AzithromycinNo adjustment
DoxycyclineNo adjustment
CeftriaxoneNo adjustment (dual hepatic/renal)
CefepimeDose-reduce; high neurotoxicity risk if not adjusted
Piperacillin-tazobactamReduce dose/interval for CrCl <40
MeropenemReduce dose/interval for CrCl <50 (seizure risk if over-dosed)
VancomycinAUC/level-guided — always individualized
LinezolidNo adjustment (monitor cytopenias)
OseltamivirReduce for CrCl <60

Thresholds are typical adult values — always confirm against your formulary and the patient's measured renal function.

Shared

Pearls & pitfalls

💡

Fourteen things that change management

  1. HCAP is dead. Don't reflexively start vancomycin + pip-tazo — cover MRSA/Pseudomonas only with validated risk factors (prior isolation, or hospitalization + IV antibiotics in 90 days).
  2. Severe CAP = 1 major (vasopressors or mechanical ventilation) or ≥3 minor criteria → ICU.
  3. Never use fluoroquinolone or macrolide monotherapy in severe CAP — a β-lactam backbone is required.
  4. Don't use procalcitonin to decide whether to start antibiotics (ProACT). It may help support stopping in improving patients.
  5. Macrolide monotherapy only where pneumococcal resistance <25% — often not true in the US (>30%).
  6. Minimum 5-day course; continue only until clinically stable + afebrile 48–72 h. Longer isn't better without complications.
  7. No routine follow-up CXR in patients improving clinically (clearing lags up to 6 weeks).
  8. No routine anaerobic coverage for aspiration unless abscess or empyema.
  9. Blood cultures + urinary antigens are for severe CAP (and MRSA/Pseudomonas-treated) — low yield otherwise.
  10. Consider hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for ICU-level severe CAP (CAPE COD) — watch glucose; not for routine non-severe CAP.
  11. ATS/IDSA prefers PSI over CURB-65 for the admit decision — but always pair the score with clinical judgment.
  12. CHF and CAP mimic and coexist — reassess the diagnosis if not responding; and remember cefepime neurotoxicity in under-dosed CKD.
  13. Test for influenza and SARS-CoV-2 when circulating; give oseltamivir to influenza-positive hospitalized patients regardless of symptom duration.
  14. De-escalate at 48 h based on cultures and clinical response — the cornerstone of stewardship.
